extracted.intended_audience: geologists, mineralogists, and readers interested in economic geology and earth-history
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and field/petrographic evidence used to decide the origin (igneous, sedimentary, metasomatic, hydrothermal) and economic status of ore deposits, illustrated with cases like Taberg, Sudbury, and Kiruna.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'ore' (economic criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'ore' usually means a material which can be profitably worked as a source of metals under existing or practicable industrial conditions; petrographers sometimes use the term more narrowly for minute mineral grains in a rock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text cites the ordinary (practical) definition and a stricter Oxford Dictionary definition (a native mineral containing a precious/useful metal in such quantity and chemical combination as to make extraction practicable). Examples: Taberg, Alno, Routivaara discussed in terms of commercial value despite mineral content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of magmatic segregation (igneous origin indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: If magnetite or other metallic minerals have been segregated into clots or masses large and pure enough to be mined, they may be considered igneous ores formed by magmatic segregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taberg is cited as an example of a magmatic segregation (magnetite concentrated centrally in hyperite), with microscopic evidence of gradual passage from normal hyperite to magnetite–olivine intergrowth. Practical economic significance depends on size and purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic granular/crystalline structure implying igneous growth
rubrics_metrics.description: A granular, crystalline intergrowth of minerals such as magnetite and olivine (rounded faces, corroded surfaces) is characteristic of growth in molten magma and supports igneous origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Törnnebohm's interpretation of Taberg uses microscopic sections showing granular intergrowth. Contrast with sharp separation and angular fragments that argue against igneous growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sharp boundaries and angular fragments indicating aqueous or secondary deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharp separations between sulphide (ore) and barren rock, and fragments with short/acute corners, indicate the ore was deposited from solution (aqueous) or as a cement filling after brecciation, rather than having crystallized in a magma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. W. Dickson's microscopic study of Sudbury shows sulphides sharply separated and fragments with short corners — used to argue for aqueous deposition during/after brecciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occurrence as cement filling in breccia and along shear planes (deposited from solution)
rubrics_metrics.description: When metallic minerals occur as cement filling interspaces between broken fragments of rock and along planes of shearing, this supports deposition from aqueous solution during/after brecciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to argue Sudbury ores are aqueous; presence of ore as cement in brecciated matrices and along shear surfaces is inconsistent with primary magmatic segregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bed-like, long-and-thin morphology suggests sedimentary or metasomatic origin
rubrics_metrics.description: Ore bodies that are much longer than broad and have a bed-like form resemble sedimentary/lode deposits rather than granular igneous segregations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kiruna ore band is nearly forty times as long as broad and appears bed-like, which the author argues is more consistent with deposition from solution or metasomatic processes than with magmatic segregation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titanium (titatic acid) content as diagnostic indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: High titanium content is associated with certain magmatic magnetite-bearing deposits (e.g., Taberg, Routivaara), whereas very low titanium suggests a different origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taberg and Routivaara ores are rich in titanic oxide and refractory/low-grade for smelting; Kiruna analyses show very low titanic acid (average ~0.23%) supporting a distinction in genesis and economic behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of adjacent/host-rock relations (field relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether surrounding rocks are igneous, sedimentary, or altered sediments and the stratigraphic/interstratified relationships are key to interpreting ore origin (syngenetic vs sedimentary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kiruna's ores occur between two series of acid rocks that have been variously interpreted; the adjacency to igneous rocks was used to dismiss a sedimentary origin in earlier debates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of ore fragments within volcanic tuffs or interbedded rocks (superficial deposition evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fragments of the ore found within tuffs or volcanic units, and interbedding with volcanic materials, can indicate that ore was deposited at/near the surface contemporaneously with or between volcanic eruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Kiruna, fragments of the ore occur in tuffs and upper porphyrite, a fact used to support theories of superficial deposition between lava flows (de Launay, Backström).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of ore deposition relative to rock consolidation (syngenetic vs epigenetic)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ore formed while the igneous host was consolidating (syngenetic), that supports magmatic segregation; if ore was deposited later than consolidation/metamorphism, that supports secondary/hydrothermal or intrusive injection models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate at Kiruna: Hogbom advocates syngenetic magmatic segregation; Stutzer describes later intrusive, banded dyke injection with pneumatolytic effects and contact impregnation — both are contrasted in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contact effects and impregnated intermediate zones (evidence for intrusive/pneumatolytic processes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Injection of ore-bearing dykes producing contact zones with impregnation of adjacent rocks supports intrusive or pneumatolytic formation of ore rather than simple stratiform deposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stutzer's view of Kiruna describes an intrusive banded dyke of magnetite+apatite whose injection produced an intermediate, impregnated zone compared to contact deposits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of petrographic and microscopic study as decisive method
rubrics_metrics.description: Microscopic section study (petrography) revealing textures, boundaries between ore and host, and mineral intergrowths is crucial evidence for distinguishing igneous vs aqueous/secondary origins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dickson (Sudbury) and examinations of Taberg and Kiruna microstructures are invoked repeatedly as primary evidence; the author relies on microscopic details to accept or reject magmatic segregation theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic viability factors affecting classification as ore
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a deposit is treated as an 'ore' depends on grade, economic tin/costs of treatment, titanium/refractory constituents, total tonnage, and remoteness affecting transport costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Taberg contains ~31% Fe in some parts but high titanium and low grade elsewhere; Alno and Routivaara deposits are of colossal size yet not economically valuable due to high titanium and remoteness; Kiruna's high-grade analyses (averages ~64% Fe) make it economically important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and origin implication (primary igneous may be deep vs aqueous limited by water penetration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ores formed from surficial waters (aqueous) are typically limited in depth to which oxygen and carbonic acid can percolate; primary igneous segregations are not so depth-limited and could increase in size downward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes economic implication: if ores are primary magmatic segregations there may be essentially no depth limit (good for future supply); if formed by surface waters they are limited to shallow depths, affecting long-term iron supply projections.
